title: Eating with Others Better for Blood Sugar — Study
paragraphs: When people think about blood sugar, they usually focus on what they eat. However, a new study from Israel suggests that who you eat with may also make a difference.

The study was carried out by researchers including Shir Atzil of the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, and it was published in the journal Science Advances in 2026. In one experiment, 108 participants ate just over 100 grams of white bread on two occasions. On one occasion, they ate alone, and on the other, they ate with a close companion, such as a partner or friend. The researchers then tracked the participants' blood sugar levels for two hours after each meal.

The results showed that when the participants ate with a companion, their blood sugar rose less sharply after the meal and returned to normal levels more quickly than when they ate alone. In other words, their bodies seemed to handle the same food more efficiently in a social setting. As Atzil put it, blood sugar control is not just about what we eat, but who we eat with.

The researchers also carried out other experiments to see how the presence of other people affects the body. When participants were exposed to cold, their bodies controlled their temperature more efficiently when a partner was present, especially if they were touching. Similarly, in a stressful situation, people's bodies reacted less strongly and recovered more quickly when another person was with them.

The researchers believe their findings support the idea that the human body is fundamentally social. Previous research has also linked loneliness to health problems such as diabetes and heart disease.

However, there are limitations. The study looked only at short-term effects, so it is not clear whether eating with others has long-term benefits. The researchers also stressed that eating with others cannot prevent or treat diabetes, and it should not replace a balanced diet, physical activity or medical care.
